headline: UNESCO Recognition Gives South Sudan's Migratory Birds a Lifeline
meta_description: Boma and Badingilo parks in South Sudan gain UNESCO World Heritage status, offering crucial protection for thousands of migratory birds crossing Africa.
summary_short: South Sudan's Boma and Badingilo national parks earned UNESCO World Heritage status in July, boosting protection for thousands of migratory birds like storks and kingfis…
body:
In July, South Sudan's Boma and Badingilo national parks and surrounding areas were designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site—a recognition that conservationists believe will prove transformative for one of Africa's most vital bird sanctuaries. The region, roughly the size of North Korea, lies at the heart of Africa's largest intact savanna system, hosting an estimated 6 million antelopes alongside some of the continent's most remarkable bird populations. The UNESCO listing is expected to attract investment and international support for conservation efforts that protect migratory species traveling thousands of kilometers between southern and northern Africa each year.

During the rainy season beginning in April, the landscape becomes a staging ground for extraordinary avian gatherings. Massive flocks of African openbills and Abdim's storks arrive to feed on abundant insects and invertebrates—snails, mollusks, and winged termites that emerge as the landscape becomes waterlogged. "There are so many storks that they kind of look like flies in the sky," said Megan Claase, a conservation manager with African Parks, which manages the parks in partnership with the South Sudanese government. Woodland kingfishers, tracked by researchers between 2016 and 2019, have been documented traveling more than 4,000 kilometers repeatedly from South African nesting sites to reach these wetlands and back again to the same trees.

Perhaps most significantly, the parks provide a haven for shoebills, enormous gray birds with hooked bills that are classified as vulnerable to extinction elsewhere across their range. In South Sudan, these charismatic species appear to thrive in healthy numbers. During a single flight over the Goum swamp in northern Boma, Claase observed up to 40 shoebills—a striking reminder of what conservation can achieve when landscape-scale protection allows birds to complete their epic continental journeys unmolested.
quick_facts: UNESCO designated Boma and Badingilo parks a World Heritage Site in July
Region hosts 6 million antelopes and approximately 470 bird species
Woodland kingfishers travel over 4,000 km between South Africa and South Sudan
Up to 40 vulnerable shoebills observed in single flight over Goum swamp
Landscape covers area roughly the size of North Korea
